title: Hospitality in the mirror
content:
[Danny Meyer](https://geni.us/dannymeyer)and [Will Guidara](https://geni.us/bYClBlK) have each written fabulous books about hospitality.

They missed one thing.

The customers who get the most authentic and lasting hospitality are the ones who deserve it.

And the ones who deserve it actually enjoy it the most.

Extraordinary hospitality offers someone more human effort and delight than they expect.

You’re not entitled to something human simply because you paid for your ticket or your table. The kids who show up on Halloween get a piece of candy, but the ritual ends there. When someone with a great costume, or singing a song or simply creating a bit of connection or magic shows up, it’s different. That’s the one we remember, the reason we answered the door and our chance to show up and return the energy. Or even a full-sized ethical chocolate bar.

For too long, the entitled customer has demanded emotional labor without offering support or sustenance in return. It’s exhausting and unfair, for both parties.

When you’re the best customer we’ve had all day, it’s likely we’ll be the host you’re hoping for.

And the best part is, that no matter how it turns out, simply trying to be the best customer of the day is its own reward. We care because we can.

# Ursula K. Le Guin on the Meaning of Life

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 34: Ursula K. Le Guin on the Meaning of Life](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/leguin_languageofthenight.jpg?fit=320%2C487&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Language-Night-Writing-Science-Fiction/dp/1668034905/?tag=braipick-20)

We are the survivors of immense and minute events — violent cosmic collisions and subtle genetic mutations, the deaths of innumerable suns and the births of innumerable cells, the splitting of continents and the splitting of atoms. Out of it all, we emerged as creatures muzzled by a consciousness that demands we give meaning to our survival. It will not come like alms dropped from the unfeeling hand of the universe. It cannot be found ready-made in the great books and the great teachers, or bought at the price of an Ivy League tuition, or sold by Silicon Valley in a ChatGPT query. That meaning is not something we find but something we make, that it is intimate as love and subjective as the reasons for it, may be the great gift and the great onus of being alive.

[Ursula K. Le Guin](https://themarginalian.org/tag/ursula-k-le-guin) (October 21, 1929–January 22, 2018) leavens the onus and magnifies the gift in a wonderful passage from her 1975 essay “Science Fiction and Mrs. Brown,” later included in her altogether magnificent collection [**_The Language of the Night: Essays on Writing, Science Fiction, and Fantasy_**](https://www.amazon.com/Language-Night-Writing-Science-Fiction/dp/1668034905/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/1405189283)).

[![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/ursulakleguin_benjaminreed_galaxy.jpg?resize=680%2C471&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Late-Day-Poems-2010-2014/dp/1629631221/braipick-20)

Ursula K. Le Guin by Benjamin Reed

With an eye to the human subject as the beating heart of the reckoning with life we call art, she writes:

> What good are all the objects in the universe, if there is no subject? It isn’t that mankind is all that important. I don’t think that [Man](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/10/17/ursula-k-le-guin-gender/) is the measure of all things, or even of very many things. I don’t think Man is the end or culmination of anything, and certainly not the center of anything. What we are, who we are, and where we are going, I do not know, nor do I believe anybody who says he knows, except, possibly, Beethoven, in the last movement of the last symphony. All I know is that we are here, and that we are aware of the fact, and that it behooves us to be aware — to pay heed. For we are not objects. That is essential… And with us, nature, the great Object, its tirelessly burning suns, its turning galaxies and planets, its rocks, seas, fish and ferns and fir trees and little furry animals, all have become, also, subjects. As we are part of them, so they are part of us. Bone of our bone, flesh of our flesh. We are their consciousness.

In this sense, the meaning of life is less like a postulate than like a poem. Half a lifetime later, Le Guin would make a beautiful distinction between [how science explicates the universe and poetry implicates it](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/04/10/ursula-k-le-guin-late-in-the-day-science-poetry/). Knowing that we are implicated in the universe and implicate it in ourselves, touching that knowledge, holding it at the center of our lives, may be the full stop beyond the question of meaning.

Complement with other beautiful perspectives on the meaning of life from [Mary Oliver](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/09/08/mary-oliver-owls/), [Oliver Sacks](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/11/08/oliver-sacks-letters-meaning-of-life/), [Loren Eiseley](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/08/11/loren-eiseley-love/), [Maya Angelou](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/29/maya-angelou-on-identity-and-the-meaning-of-life/), and [Fyodor Dostoyevsky](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/12/05/dostoyevsky-execution-life/), then revisit Le Guin on [how to live fully](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/05/24/le-guin-lathe-of-heaven-change/).

# Nathaniel Hawthorne on How to Look and Really See

### By Maria Popova

“One can’t write directly about the soul,” Virginia Woolf [wrote](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/02/06/virginia-woolf-soul-aging/). “Looked at, it vanishes.” This is true of any soul — our own, that of another, that of the world. It vanishes because whenever we look, we see not as reality is but as we are. We see the rest of nature — [including each other](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/09/20/eudora-welty-photography/) — through eyes gauzed with preconception, our distracted vision blurred by the thousand thoughts that come alive before the mind’s eye at any given moment, more vivid than the living reality before us.

A lovely recipe for how to see the world more clearly comes from **Nathaniel Hawthorne** (July 4, 1804–May 19, 1864) — perhaps a lesser novelist than Woolf, but a greater one than Melville in Melville’s own estimation, [lovesick as he was](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/02/13/herman-melville-nathaniel-hawthorne-love-letters/), and a far greater observer of nature in his novels than all the journaling Transcendentalists combined. When Thoreau looked at nature, he saw only metaphor and parable; when Hawthorne looked, he saw nature on its own terms, letting it mirror back the fractal of itself that is human nature as the light of unfiltered awareness fell on it. In that respect, he was more a Buddhist than a Transcendentalist, more a scientist than a novelist, and always a poet of reality.

![Image 34](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/nathanielhawthorne.jpg?resize=680%2C950&ssl=1)

Nathaniel Hawthorne

In the high summer of 1851 — a year after _The Scarlet Letter_ interrupted Hawthorne’s long obscurity to catapult the middle-aged author into celebrity — he took his five-year-old son Julian to the lake near the little red shanty they had rented in the Berkshires. Sitting at the water’s edge, Hawthorne wrote in a journal entry later included in Julian’s tender two-volume biography of his parents, [**_Nathaniel Hawthorne and His Wife_**](https://www.amazon.com/Nathaniel-Hawthorne-His-Wife-Biography/dp/1313031291/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://www.worldcat.org/title/nathaniel-hawthorne-and-his-wife-a-biography/oclc/42262393&referer=brief_results) | [_public domain_](https://archive.org/details/nathanielhawthor01hawt_0)):

> The best way to get a vivid impression and feeling of a landscape, is to sit down before it and read, or become otherwise absorbed in thought; for then, when your eyes happen to be attracted to the landscape, you seem to catch Nature unawares, and see her before she has time to change her aspect. The effect lasts but for a single instant, and passes away almost as soon as you are conscious of it; but it is real, for that moment. It is as if you could overhear and understand what the trees are whispering to one another; as if you caught a glimpse of a face unveiled, which veils itself from every willful glance. The mystery is revealed, and after a breath or two, becomes just as great a mystery as before.

[![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Nebular_by_MariaPopova.jpg?resize=680%2C680&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/nebular7042035_print?curator=brainpicker)

_Nebular_ by Maria Popova. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/nebular7042035_print?curator=brainpicker), benefitting The Nature Conservancy)

Complement with James Baldwin on [the revelation that taught him to truly see](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/18/james-baldwin-writers-chapbook-revelation/) and Georgia O’Keeffe on [the art of seeing](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/11/15/georgia-okeeffe-flower/), then revisit Hawthorne on [the edges of consciousness](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/08/22/nathaniel-hawthorne-the-haunted-mind/) and his stirring meditation on [life, death, and what fills the interlude with meaning](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/11/18/nathaniel-hawthorne-una/), composed while watching his young daughter interact with his dying mother.

# Introducing the Museum of Delight

### By Maria Popova

After twenty years of making immaterial things with my mind — ideas sculpted of words, questions woven of sentences, translucent vessels for thought and feeling in the shape of poems — I found myself overcome by the urge to make things with my hands out of matter: clay, thread, stone, resin, wood, lichen.

They now live in the Museum of Delight.

![Image 47](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/mod_sign_big.jpg?resize=680%2C477&ssl=1)

Housed in a decommissioned airstream from the 1950s that took a year to transform, the Museum of Delight is a collaboration with my friend and neighbor [Ryan Vahey](https://ryanvahey.com/) — a multidisciplinary artist who lost his entire life’s work and all of his equipment as he watched his studio burn to the ground in the [ferocious fire](https://www.instagram.com/p/DPC34jGkaa6/?psln=cXA5MW1rczk3dWZt) that lit up our neighborhood with the glaring reminder that anything can change for any one of us at any given moment.

Like a museum, the Museum of Delight constellates objects into an experience; unlike a museum, and more like an art gallery, you can have what is in it; unlike a gallery, you can’t buy anything, but you can have some things if chance smiles upon you: Each time the Museum of Delight is open, eleven objects in it will be given away in a pay-what-you-wish raffle. You can enter it in person or remotely by [making a donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/) in any amount commensurate with your ability and level of delight, so long as it ends with the decimal .11. (The loveliness of a lottery is the antipode to the rich-getting-richer ugliness of art world auctions: Whether you enter with $1.11 or $10,000.11, your odds are the same — the only difference is by how much you support this labor of love, all the thousands of hours and thousands of dollars poured into making these constellations of matter, into turning waste to wonder.)

![Image 48](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MoD_build4.jpg?resize=680%2C510&ssl=1)

![Image 49](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/mod4.jpg?resize=680%2C617&ssl=1)

Proceeds from the raffle will also help Ryan rebuild his life: delight as the counterforce to destruction.

![Image 50](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MoD_build1.jpg?resize=680%2C510&ssl=1)

![Image 51](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MoD_build2.jpg?resize=680%2C510&ssl=1)

![Image 52](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/mod2.jpg?resize=680%2C680&ssl=1)

![Image 54](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/mod1.jpg?resize=680%2C831&ssl=1)

![Image 55](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/hand1.jpg?resize=680%2C794&ssl=1)

The Museum of Delight, which opens its space-age door at the [twentieth anniversary celebration of _The Marginalian_](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/live) tomorrow, will be touring New York City and Upstate New York in the coming months, making its next stop at Woodstock’s beloved Japanese restaurant [Medo](https://medowoodstock.com/) on Sunday, October 25, 1PM-4PM. More stops will be announced [on this page](https://www.themarginalian.org/museum-of-delight/). (If you have a dining establishment in New York City, which apparently is the only place this felictious colossus can be parked without a special permit, and you would like to host the Museum of Delight for an afternoon or evening, please [contact Ryan](mailto:rvahey@gmail.com).) # How to Hold Your Heart with Golden Hands

### By Maria Popova

One bleak English winter a long time ago, wandering through London in the wake of a relationship that had just unraveled, I walked into an antiquarian bookstore and chanced upon a rare century-old edition of the Brothers Grimm fairy tales — which I had grown up with — illustrated by [Arthur Rackham](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/arthur-rackham/).

[![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/arthurrackham_grimm27.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/29/arthur-rackham-brothers-grimm/)

All fairy tales deal in enchantment, but the Grimms’ are especially powerful cautionary tales about [the treacherous line between true and false enchantment in love](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/24/love-enchantment/) — something [Rackham’s art](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/29/arthur-rackham-brothers-grimm/) captured exquisitely.

One particular illustration stopped me up short, unnerved me, captivated me with its disquieting fusion of terror and tenderness:

[![Image 38](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/arthurrackham_grimm5.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/29/arthur-rackham-brothers-grimm/)

The image haunted me for years. I kept returning to it, puzzling over what it was telling me. I lived more, I loved more, and eventually came to see it as a perfect and terrible metaphor for what happens when two people with attachment trauma mistake their trauma for love. Most relationships fail and falter out of this confusion, whatever its manifestation. Here, in this century-old illustration, was a key to an elemental truth: You cannot hold, or hold on to, anyone else unless you can hold yourself — hold your own heart, hold the roots of your pain, whatever it may be — with absolute golden compassion.

I wanted a response to Rackham, a counterpoint, something to visualize the power of that truth, so I set out to make it.

I began wandering forests and shorelines, looking for driftwood and windthrow trees, exerting inordinate joules taking off their centuries-old roots and giant burls with my Japanese hand-saw, spending inordinate hours sanding them and polishing them with urushi lacquer, then making for them small ceramic hands covered in kintsugi gold powder.

![Image 39](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/wood_MariaPopova2.jpg?resize=680%2C383&ssl=1)

![Image 40](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/wood_MariaPopova1.jpg?resize=680%2C383&ssl=1)

![Image 41](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/wood_MariaPopova3.jpg?resize=680%2C383&ssl=1)

They now live in the [Museum of Delight](https://www.themarginalian.org/museum-of-delight/) as large-scale reminders that we spend our whole lives learning how to hold our own hearts.

title: Noema’s AI Reading List
content:
Credits

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

AI’s climb up the capability ladder is moving more rapidly, even exponentially, than its progenitors expected. To keep up and put it in perspective, Noema has compiled a [reading list](https://www.noemamag.com/noemas-ai-reading-list/) of our best essays and interviews from a couple of years ago through the present. No doubt, we will need a new list again a few months down the road.

For now, here is a resource for following the trajectory of the most important technological breakthrough of this century so far.

![Image 1](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2026/04/blackout_no4_julesjulien-scaled.png?fm=png&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=69d7c696e23a980a83ce8ac35a4182e3)

Jules Julien for Noema Magazine

1. [**How To Future-Proof Your Career In The Age Of AI**](https://www.noemamag.com/why-a-liberal-arts-education-will-soon-be-more-valuable-than-ever/)

The most prized workers will be those who can decode a sea of outputs, spot the meaningful signal and translate it into action that others understand and trust.

**by Nils Gilman**

![Image 2](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2026/09/illustration-Bright-Woo-scaled.jpg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=0949896613440e298202474a2fce73b8)

Bright Woo for Noema Magazine

2. [**Whose AI Will Rule The World**](https://www.noemamag.com/whose-ai-will-rule-the-world/)

As AI changes everything, the Chinese seem more optimistic than the Americans. Why?

**by Jacob Dreyer**

![Image 3](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2026/06/noema-new.jpg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=2d5add7bba00beb4210fc3c5d564137d)

Musubu Hagi for Noema Magazine

3. [**How AI Will Change Us**](https://www.noemamag.com/how-ai-will-change-us)

When the most patient, well-read, emotionally responsive conversationalist in the world is always available, what will we still need from one another?

**by Houda Nait El Barj**

![Image 4](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2026/09/2024_01_SERIFA_David_Autor.jpg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=c8c32ca5c804d9181aaf5ccc586578cd)

SERIFA for Noema Magazine

4. [**AI Could Actually Help Rebuild The Middle Class**](https://www.noemamag.com/how-ai-could-help-rebuild-the-middle-class/)

AI doesn’t have to be a job destroyer. It offers us the opportunity to extend expertise to a larger set of workers.

**by David Autor**

[Video 5](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/assets-noemamag.com/2024/05/NOEMA_DOTS_WEB.mp4)

Shalinder Matharu for Noema Magazine

5. [**When AIs Develop Their Own Language, Pull The Plug**](https://www.noemamag.com/mapping-ais-rapid-advance/)

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt weighs in on where AI is headed, when to “pull the plug” and how to cope with China.

**A conversation with Eric Schmidt**

![Image 5: An illustration by Matthieu Bourel for Noema Magazine.](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2025/04/FINAL_947wx1186h_px_300dpi.jpg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=261d3b9d97986a5b99e707ba7f134bde)

Matthieu Bourel for Noema Magazine

6. [**Here’s How To Share AI’s Future Wealth**](https://www.noemamag.com/heres-how-to-share-ais-future-wealth/)

Advanced AI threatens to increase inequality and concentrate power, but we can proactively distribute AI’s benefits to foster a just and inclusive economy before it’s too late.

**by Saffron Huang and Sam Manning**

![Image 6](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2024/05/RGB-1.jpg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=8f1ca627d909c1c60821ee9e3e55ba85)

Setu Choudhary for Noema Magazine

7. [**The Danger Of Superhuman AI Is Not What You Think**](https://www.noemamag.com/the-danger-of-superhuman-ai-is-not-what-you-think/)

The rhetoric over “superhuman” AI implicitly erases what’s most important about being human.

**by Shannon Vallor**

![Image 7](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2026/06/Merijn-Hos-x-Noema-Final.jpg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=52fafab72bef343344063706895df469)

Merijn Hos for Noema Magazine

8. **[When The Machines Deserve Our Consideration](https://www.noemamag.com/when-the-machines-deserve-our-consideration/)**

We will never know for sure if AI can be conscious. A neuroscientist argues that we shouldn’t wait for proof to decide how to treat it.

**by Grigori Guitchounts**

![Image 8](https://noemamag.imgix.net/2026/03/F005-ocre.jpg?fm=pjpg&ixlib=php-3.3.1&s=5bf6b486ca3991a604ffae09edb70656)

Matthieu Bourel for Noema Magazine

9. [**The Devastating Mistake Employers Are Making When It Comes To AI Understanding Of Intelligence**](https://www.noemamag.com/what-the-ai-consciousness-question-conceals/)

They are confusing efficiency for intelligence and the absence of friction with the presence of thought.

**by Barton Friedland**

Andreion De Castro for Noema Magazine

Today’s tech “prophets” push a narrative that God-like artificial superintelligence is inevitable, and only they can ensure humanity’s safety from their creations.

**by James O’Sullivan**

title: Sudan As A Mirror For Today’s World
content:
Credits

Alden Young is an associate professor of history and global affairs at Yale University. He was a 2021-22 Berggruen Institute Fellow.

Muez Ali is an adjunct professor at Georgetown University in Qatar and honorary research fellow at University College London.

This work is supported by the Cross-Border Conflict Evidence, Policy and Trends (XCEPT) research program, funded by UK International Development. The views and opinions expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily represent those of the UK government.

Sudan has often served as a mirror for judging the health of the liberal world order because it has repeatedly been a laboratory for multilateral interventions to prevent atrocities and stabilize the humanitarian situation.

During the second Sudanese civil war, which stretched from 1983 to 2005, an estimated more than [two million](https://media.defense.gov/2025/Feb/25/2003651741/-1/-1/0/20250204_SECONDSUDAN_1983-2005.PDF) people died. In Darfur during the first decade of the 2000s, international observers estimated that 300,000 people died and another 2-3 million people were displaced.

At the time, finding a solution to Sudan’s conflicts was a priority for the United States and the coalitions it galvanized. For instance, Sudan’s second civil war came to an end only after intense mediation by the troika of the United States, the United Kingdom and Norway, as well as Sudan’s African neighbors, in 2005. The level of Western concern and diplomatic resources mobilized to intervene in Sudan’s conflicts in the early 2000s feels almost unimaginable today.

In the 2000s, Sudan hosted two massive UN peacekeeping [missions](https://peacekeeping.un.org/en/past-peacekeeping-operations): the more than 13-year-long African Union-United Nations Hybrid Operation in Darfur, which ended in 2020 and the more than six-year-long United Nations Mission in the Sudan, which ended in 2011. The goals of these missions were to prevent genocide in Darfur and to guarantee the implementation of the peace agreement ending the civil war between the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement/Army and the government in Khartoum. This mission, which included approximately 10,000 soldiers and numerous civilian authorities, ended with a referendum on the independence of South Sudan in 2011. A few months later South Sudan was welcomed by the international community as the newest country in the world.

It was in this context — of the international efforts to end Sudan’s civil wars and the resulting mass displacements — that South Sudanese diplomat Francis Mading Deng developed the idea of “[sovereignty as responsibility](https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.7864/j.ctv80cc8b).” Deng served as the Special Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General on internally displaced persons from 1992 to 2004, and many experts [credit](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/international-theory/article/recovering-african-contestation-and-innovation-in-global-politics-francis-deng-and-sovereigntyasresponsibility/F96F40C4838701F48B3DBD67E0A882E9?utm_date=20241118&utm_id=1731917430&utm_c) Deng’s idea of sovereignty as responsibility as the intellectual genesis of the international principle of the [Responsibility to Protect](https://www.un.org/fr/node/218466). The UN General Assembly’s adoption of the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principles in 2005 marked a high-water point for the legitimacy of the liberal world order. R2P, as formulated by Deng and others, tried to balance sovereignty as a state’s right to non-interference with the international community’s duty to ensure that a state protects the welfare of its own citizens.

Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm. The numbers are massive and stark, making it hard to comprehend the magnitude of the tragedy unfolding there. At least 14 million people have [been internally displaced](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/04/1167281) since the latest round of fighting in April 2023, according to the United Nations Refugee Agency. Meanwhile, there are at least 4.4 million Sudanese refugees who have fled the country, many to neighboring countries like Chad, Egypt and South Sudan, which can ill-afford to support this influx. Three years on, intense fighting persists in Sudan’s central region of Kordofan, in Darfur and in its southeastern Blue Nile state.

In one of the most widely discussed recent commentaries on the crisis in Sudan — a conflict often overshadowed despite its horrific violence by other wars — the American journalist and historian Anne Applebaum wrote that “no statistics can express the sense of pointlessness, of meaninglessness, that the war has left behind” after she [reported](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2025/09/sudan-civil-war-humanitarian-crisis/683563/) from behind the lines of both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and their opponents, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). In the face of the physical destruction of cities like Khartoum, Applebaum declared the conflict the most nihilistic on Earth, writing with a tinge of hopelessness that “the liberal world order has already ended in Sudan, and there isn’t anything to replace it.”

In many ways, what is happening in Sudan represents the international community’s abandonment of the longstanding principles of the liberal world order, particularly by the West. Instead, Sudan has become the plaything for a wide array of actors stretching across the Middle East and Africa, to Russia and Ukraine, and as far afield as Colombia. After the Trump administration’s cuts to organizations like the U.S. Agency for International Development, even the [commitment](https://www.noemamag.com/what-comes-after-the-refugee-camp/) to prevent the spread of famine has declined. Applebaum ended her piece by lamenting that Sudan is now a victim of an anarchic, post-American world. A world that has yet to fully take shape in which “colonialism is long past, the Cold War has ended,” and the international order has irreparably broken down.

> “Today, the conflict in Sudan can be described as a world war in microcosm.”

But what is taking place in Sudan and elsewhere is not the emergence of anarchy; it is a return to precolonial patterns. Many observers have mistakenly assumed the former because of what the historian Richard Reid calls the “[foreshortening of African history](https://www.jstor.org/stable/23017673),” by which he means “the detachment of Africa’s turbulent present — and its recent past — from deeper patterns of both change and continuity.” Perhaps no country has suffered more from the reification of the colonial past by social scientists and modernizing elites alike than the Congo, once known as Zaire.

At the end of the 19th century, Henry Morten Stanley earned the name _Bula Matari_ or the breaker of rocks, for “his feat of driving a caravan of porters bearing dismantled steamers over the torturous terrain between the Zaire River estuary and the vast navigable watercourses extending inward from Kinshasa.” As Zala Lusibu N’Kanza, the first woman to hold the position of minister in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, notes, “for all Bakongo the name of Bula Matari signified terror.” The precolonial was smashed in the wake of an ascendant and modernizing colonial and post-colonial state. For the founding generation of American political scientists like the late Crawford Young, the political, economic and social institutions of the precolonial period were left in ruins because they lacked the resilience to create an alternative to the modernizing state.

## A Return To The Pre-Colonial Era

Despite the depths of the human tragedy playing out across northeast Africa — engulfing not only Sudan but South Sudan, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Somalia and Somaliland — Applebaum’s post-American world is not just chaos. Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era. The long dominance of the colonial state was not the result of smashing African societies, as American political scientists long suspected. Just as the chaos marring the post-colonial period is not a result of ethnic rivalries. Rather, the endurance of colonialism in countries like Sudan is a product of the legacies of its infrastructure.

The peculiar durability of the infrastructure built during European control of the Nile basin resulted from a set of historical conjunctures. In his new book, “The Alibi of Capital: How We Broke the Earth to Steal the Future on the Promise of a Better Tomorrow,” the political theorist Timothy Mitchell argues that around the turn of the 20th century a new ability to discount the future was invented. Mitchell considers this ability a political technology “derived from the fact that time can be controlled — by the construction of a political apparatus that will reliably capture and colonize the future.” While this sounds incredibly abstract, Mitchell goes on to explain that:

“That the scale and extension of transportation lines and energy networks, along with urban development, irrigation projects, and other immense schemes, depended not just on material durability but upon the durable arrangements of law, authority, compulsion, and justification.”

Sudan, though often imagined as a colonial backwater, was the site of one of the British Empire’s largest investments in industrial agriculture ever. The giant Gezira irrigated agricultural scheme, one of the only monuments to colonialism visible from outer space, was originally planned in the 1920s to irrigate more than a million acres. British officials spoke openly of the Gezira Scheme’s potential to be a second man-made Nile Delta, a giant cotton farm for the Empire. From the 1920s until the scheme ran into financial problems in the 1970s, the railways, dams, ports and even Sudan’s labor force were geared to serve this project, not to mention the country’s financial and economic infrastructure.

This changed in the 1990s as the oil sector rose to prominence, but even then, pipelines and refineries tended to be located according to [patterns](https://books.google.co.za/books?hl=en&lr=&id=dwsnDAAAQBAJ&oi=fnd&pg=PP1&dq=oil+pipelines+sudan+colonialism&ots=J51itG_uCa&sig=H2wXEAYVmDwaAu8Ad8NlEcsi3Ro&redir_esc=y#v=onepage&q&f=false) established during the colonial era. These patterns endured in part because irrigation canals and railways cut into the earth and were reinforced with steel, and because Sudan integrated into global financial markets through loans for investments backed by access to export markets. Originally, it was cotton, later crude oil and now gold.

## The Fragile Liberal International Order

When the Princeton political scientist G. John Ikenberry wrote about the liberal international order, he [remarked](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/perspectives-on-politics/article/abs/liberal-internationalism-30-america-and-the-dilemmas-of-liberal-world-order/129F6B11B2E3A7AA8DDBCE18362D9163) that, “there is an optimist assumption lurking in liberal internationalism that states can overcome constraints and cooperate to solve security dilemmas, pursue collective action, and create an open, stable system.” Yet Ikenberry also admits that the system’s collective nature was always more aspirational than practical. Ikenberry admits that since 1945 the United States has served as the owner and operator of this system and has been afforded special privileges and responsibilities. Applebaum describes the chaos that unfolds in Sudan once the United States is no longer willing to bear its historic burden.

> “Clear patterns are emerging even amid the violence of state fracture. One of the clearest is the development of political and trade patterns resembling those of the pre-colonial era.”

But what if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable? While cotton and crude petroleum are different commodities, the central state could largely control their export, either by managing production directly or by issuing licenses for production and sale to favored clients. The boom in gold exports from Sudan since 2013 is remarkable because of the state’s utter inability to control the trade. For Sudan, the tragedy is magnified by the almost 200% [rise](https://www.bullionbypost.com/gold-price/10-year-gold-price-chart-usd/) in gold prices during that period, meaning the Sudanese state lost out on this windfall due to incapacity and now war. Part of the challenge for Sudanese authorities is that [artisanal gold production](https://noria-research.com/mena/black-gold-liquid-metal-the-political-economy-of-gold-in-sudan/), unlike control of oilfields and pipelines or cotton irrigation, lacks the central infrastructural chokepoints the colonial and postcolonial state had become so adept at taxing.

The other dilemma for the Sudanese state is the regional collapse of the taboo against dealing with subnational actors. As a result, gold from the mines of Darfur often ends up in the souks of Dubai without ever passing through the central government. Similarly, Sudanese soldiers guarding the Saudi-Yemeni border can be hired and deployed without ever contracting with the SAF. The RSF, a paramilitary-slash-merchant company, carries out many of these transactions, managing large portions of Sudan on behalf of its investors.

## Precolonial Patterns Return In Contemporary Guises

What looks like chaos reveals patterns. In the 3 ½ years since fighting broke out between the SAF and the RSF, new trade and military supply routes have become increasingly visible. During the first few decades following Sudan’s independence in 1956, most economic activity flowed from the provinces to Khartoum, then along the railroad lines to Port Sudan on the Red Sea. The government earned most of its revenue by taxing the imports and exports that followed this well-trodden route. During the first two years of fighting, the Rapid Support Forces controlled Khartoum and did everything in their power to break the old colonial trade route. During this time, Sudan’s government retreated to Port Sudan, and the RSF set up a rival capital in Nyala in southern Darfur.

Inadvertently, the war revealed older patterns of state formation from the 19th century. Sudan’s city of Suakin and its other Red Sea ports claimed allegiance to a distant Ottoman government and resisted incorporation into the Kingdom of Sennar, to say nothing of Darfur. Elites in Suakin often sought incorporation into the Ottoman province of the Hijaz or Aden on the Arabian Peninsula. This pattern threatened to repeat itself when Sudan’s government was again temporarily forced to relocate to Port Sudan after Khartoum fell in 2023.

But perhaps more dramatically, the war saw the re-emergence of old trade routes to the north, west and south of Darfur. With the SAF in control of Port Sudan, the RSF began to turn to the old trade routes across the desert, the most famous of which was the Darb El Arba’īn, or “40 Day Road,” leading from northern Darfur to Asyut in southern Egypt. Other trade routes led north into Libya, where the RSF is [suspected](https://www.info-res.org/articles/how-we-found-an-rsf-military-camp-in-the-libyan-desert/) to have established bases under the protection of the Libyan militia leader who rules the eastern part of the country, Khalifa Haftar. Similarly, the trading routes from southern Darfur into South Sudan have been reactivated to resupply the RSF. These routes often end in Uganda, Kenya and the Central African Republic. All outside the control of the center.

The new prominence of the old trade routes was capped by the declaration of [TASIS](https://tasissudan.com/tasis-announces-formation-of-government-of-peace-and-unity/), or the Sudan Founding Alliance, of a new government in April 2025, exactly two years after the outbreak of the war. Speaking from Nairobi, Kenya’s capital, TASIS leaders tried to solidify an alliance between the RSF, parts of the Sudanese People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), a militant group and political party, and the leadership of the [Baggara](https://www.101lasttribes.com/tribes/baggara.html) confederation. The Baggara includes more than six million Arab and African people stretching from southern Kordofan to Lake Chad.

The RSF’s organization, founded in 2013 — with the Darfurian Arab family of its leader Muhammad Hamdan Daglo Musa at its center — itself echoes an episode from the late 19th century. The first is the creation of a private-merchant empire by al-Zubayr Rahma al-Mansur, usually known as [Zubayr Pasha](https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20200728-zubair-pasha-remembered/). Originally a lackluster merchant assistant for an Egyptian trader, by the 1860s Zubayr had established one of the largest merchant companies operating in what we today refer to as South Sudan.

His operations were [described](https://www.middleeastmonitor.com/20200728-zubair-pasha-remembered/) in a remembrance in the “Middle East Monitor” as such: “[He sent] men ‘through the lands of the Dinka, Jur and Bongo, the company reached the Golo, then living between the Kuru and Kpongo rivers.’ They purchased ostrich feathers and ivory for trade in Khartoum, Cairo and beyond.” By the 1870s, he had grown from a successful trader into the ruler of a territory often called Deim Zubayr, controlling a large area of present-day South Sudan’s Bahr al-Ghazal and Darfur with an army of some 12,000 soldiers, many of whom were enslaved. According to the historian [Tsega Etefa](https://www.colgate.edu/about/directory/tetefa), writing in the Journal of Oromo Studies:

> “What if what looks like chaos is simply the dissolution of the political orders that made colonial and postcolonial state investments durable?”

“By the late 1860s, al Zubayr was ‘the most prominent and successful of the merchant princes operating in the Bahr al-Ghazal.’ He traded in slaves and ivory; however, antislavery movements by Egyptian and European explorers in the Nile Valley began to put pressure on him. Therefore, ‘he arranged with the Baqqara tribes of southern Darfur for his slave caravans to pass through their territory northward, bypassing the Nile.’ Toward the end of the 1860s, ‘he attained the position of practically an independent ruler.’ The Egyptian government’s expeditionary force ‘was completely defeated by him, and the Egyptian authorities, realizing with what a commanding character they were confronted, made him Governor of the district.’”

Initially, Zubayr’s base was in the southern borderlands between Darfur and Bahr al-Ghazal. Darfur, as an independent political entity, was not conquered until 1874, when Zubayr’s forces achieved what the Ottoman-Egyptian armies of Muhammad Ali had been unable to do in 1821: conquering the Fur Sultanate at its capital of El Fasher. The parallels with the RSF appear to write themselves. These became particularly notable when the RSF took El Fasher after months of siege at the end of October 2025. In the process, the RSF captured the last major stronghold in Darfur and solidified their ability to resupply to the north through Libya and to the south across the expanse of South Sudan into East Africa.

Yet another echo of the 19th century was the emergence of Kordofan as a contested region. The armies of Muhammad Ali, de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, partially pacified the region in the decades after the 1821 invasion from Egypt, but could not maintain stable control. In many ways, this resembles the situation in Kordofan today, where cities like [El-Obeid](https://refugees.org/no-safe-haven-displacement-survival-in-el-obeid/), with a population over 600,000, remain under frequent attack as rival forces contend to dominate the region. Still, the 19th-century echoes perhaps become clearest in the relative autonomy of the SPLM-N, a political party and militant group with its strongholds based in southern Kordofan.

The SPLM-N has been both a broker and spoiler for South Sudan since its secession in 2011. The flat plains were easily conquered, but the Nuba Mountains were very difficult to ultimately control. One faction, SPLM-N Al-Hilu, which mostly controls the areas around the Nuba Mountains in South Kordofan, sided with the RSF, while another faction, SPLM-N Agar, which controls parts of the Blue Nile state, has sided with the SAF.

In the process, the two groups have maintained the autonomy of the border regions between the RSF, SAF and South Sudan. A borderland organization more interested in preserving its own autonomy than in the outcome of the war has found itself operating on both sides of the conflict. In this way, they are implementing strategies with other surprising parallels in the past, such as the [Kingdom of Taqali](https://www.jstor.org/stable/178832?seq=2), a kingdom in the northeastern Nuba Mountains of Sudan that flourished between about 1780 and 1884, with relative autonomy that extended well into Sudan’s post-independence period until 1969.

Our research in the Sudan Collection at the University of Bergen in Norway shows that during the 19th century, Taqali leaders used a similar strategy of seeking protection and recognition from both the waning states of Darfur and Sennar —pledging vassalage to both simultaneously as they worked to maintain autonomy.

The breakdown of the Sudanese state we are witnessing today is also not random. Rather, along with the retreat of the liberal world order, we are witnessing the reappearance of political orders that last manifested themselves with such clarity in the 19th century. These patterns repeat because they are based on trade and political and economic linkages that do not rely on the infrastructure built during the colonial period. The durability of this infrastructure has decayed as the institutions of the liberal world order that maintained it have crumbled. In the place of the patterns of trade, infrastructure and political order that once felt like inevitable parts of the postcolonial world, we are witnessing the reappearance of the older routes of exchange.

For instance, we see the re-emergence of the Trans-Saharan routes, the trading routes into East and Central Africa and East-West connections across the Sahel and the Red Sea. In South Africa, there are calls to dissolve the Union of South Africa, which in 1910 joined the British Cape Colony with the independent Boer republics of the Transvaal and Free State as well as Natal. Yemen has been redividing for over a decade now in ways that are reminiscent of the 19th century, and of course Russian aggression has called into question the stability of eastern Europe’s borders.

These are just a few examples of how the stability that defined the second half of the 20th century cannot be taken for granted. As we think of what models might best explain statecraft after the liberal order, it increasingly makes sense to look at the 19th-century map as an example of political competition and shifting boundaries.

title: Moralized Trends Are Often Extended
content:
Compared to the ancients, we moderns less moralize our personal lives, but more moralize the bigger world around us. Wars and politics, for example, are more moralized to us. In particular, we tend to be eager to interpret big-scale trends in moral terms, and often do so if enough trend context factors can support such an interpretation. These moral interpretations often change how we respond to big tends, which often enhances these trends.

For example, when gas prices rise, many are tempted to explain this as due to a rise in the selfishness of oil executives. Which can make them push for price controls and regulations that over time tend to cause higher gas prices. Similarly, rising costs of housing are often attributed to greedy landlords and developers, resulting in price controls and regulations that make it less attractive to build or rent housing, and so higher housing prices.

On the other side, for trends like rises in school and medical spending, more attention to kids, less corporal punishment of kids, and delayed marriages, it is possible to frame them as due to increasing clarity, resolve, or knowledge re virtues and moral truths. Even if initially caused by other contextual factors, such moral interpretations can induce people to more admire those who do such things, and to do more of them themselves. Which extends those trends.

This process add a multiplier effect to the efforts of cultural activists seeking to induce moral changes. Once they can cause any visible trend, using most any available means, the world many respond to that trend via an interpretation of changed morals, when then adds force to the change trend.

Compared to the ancients, the modern world does more of this because we are more eager to moralize big trends, and we have a lot more faster big changes in context.

(This post is an attempt to simplify and generalize my [last post](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/mistaking-context-for-virtue).)

title: Mistaking Context for Virtue
content:
Imagine taking a big group of elites from the year 1700, giving them the tech, wealth, and economic options of today, also teaching them new facts that we have learned since then, but without putting them in contact with the people of today. If they held their values constant, and only adapted their behavior to these ways to achieve constant values, they would change many of their behaviors to adapt to this new context. However, it seems to me that their behaviors would be quite different from those of people today with the same facts, tech, wealth, and economic options. That (big) difference shows how our values have in effect changed since 1700.

I’ve been puzzling over what could have caused such huge fast value changes. I had been attributing much of it to cultural activism, but on reflection we’ve seen many apparent value changes in areas that seem to have little activism. For example, few seem to have advocated for the switch from cornerstone to capstone marriage. What else could cause such big change?

Consider three related facts. First, we tend to copy the behaviors and attitudes of elites, i.e., people we admire, and also to give them the benefit of doubts re their motives. Second, our book The Elephant in the Brain argues that most of us are quite badly informed on our motives re many key areas of life. Third, decades of psychology has found that we tend to neglect context in favor of intrinsic personal attributes when explaining behavior. Some have called this our “fundamental attribution error”. Values are important examples of personal attributes.

These facts tempt me to consider the following hypothesis: when elites change behaviors associated with virtue, observers tend to neglect context explanations of those changes in favor of value explanations. That is, observers, including the elites themselves, tend to attribute changed elite virtue behaviors to their more strongly or clearly expressing certain values. And perhaps even to their having discovered new related moral truths. This clearer elite demonstration and endorsement of those values induces observers to want to also more strongly and clearly express them.

For example, imagine that due to increasing wealth, falling family size, and stronger educational competition, elite parents switched to spending more time with their kids, a behavior widely seen as virtuous. Observers will interpret this as stronger clearer signals that spending time with kids is widely accepted as virtuous. Such observers will then be induced to spend more time with kids, which will make them feel and seem more virtuous. And that will confirm to those elite parents the strong and accepted virtue of spending time with kids.

This process amplifies the initial change in elite parental attention, pushing toward a larger overall change in parental attention, attributed to a new moral revelation: past parents were morally bad in neglecting their kids. Thank goodness new parents now see the moral truth that good parents are constantly with their kids.

The same process could happen re the switch from cornerstone to capstone marriage. Elites’ initially delayed marriage due to longer educational paths, but then the new models of elite marriage changed the shared image of the ideal marriage as one of mature people who know themselves well choosing others who match them well. And then the more that respected elites do this, the more it confirms for all that this is what virtuous people do. Bad people, in contrast, get married too young.

If this process has been common through history, it would have amplified most any ways that elites seem to more value some things. But when such changes were small, their amplifications would also have been small. Maybe what is distinct about the modern era is just how common are large changes in behavior due to big changes in the contexts of tech, wealth, social interaction scales, etc.

title: Five Slogans Re Cultural Drift
content:
I’m wondering how well I might organize my [cultural](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/our-big-oops?utm_source=publication-search)[drift](https://quillette.com/2024/04/11/beware-cultural-drift/) messages around a few key slogans. Consider the following slogans as placeholders for better worded versions.

Humanity’s superpower is cultural evolution. But such Darwinian evolution fails without sufficient variation or selection pressures, or if the context changes too fast. A few centuries ago we were fine; the world had 100Ks of peasant cultures, most facing frequent wars, pandemics, and famines, in an economy that took a millennia to double. But then we merged peasants into a hundred or so national cultures, and then those into just a few world cultures, all of which got so rich, healthy and peaceful that they almost never die. Also, the world economy now doubles every twenty years, fifty times faster than before. So now we are likely in trouble.

Every cultural feature has a min scale at which it can vary; below that scale, people have to do it the same. We are doing fine re features that can vary at small scales, but in trouble re features that set game-theoretic equilibria, and so can only vary at large scales. Features of corporate culture are small enough, but global features are not. Our actions are nested in goal hierarchies, and our most troubled cultural features correspond to basic goals, near key values and morals, which are hard to vary locally as cultures punish moral deviants.

A reasonable response to evolution failing re our more basic goals would be to become conservative about changing them. Allow changes to means, which can easily vary at small scales, but not to the ends which direct such means. That is, change hows but not whys. [Alas](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/innovation-without-feedback-is-drift), humanity moved the other way. At the dawn of “modernity”, the status jump that STEM (including business) fields had won via innovation inspired non-STEM fields like art, religion, philosophy, politics, etc. to also embrace innovation. Even though they mostly didn’t see enough data to pick adaptive changes.

Embracing a [folk morality](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/prefer-evolved-to-folk-morality), our most celebrated heroes are now the cultural activists who cause the greatest changes to values and morals. As a result, we are decaying into maladaption far faster than we otherwise would. The clearest example of such decay is falling fertility; peak world babies/yr was in 2016, and world population will start to fall in ~30yrs, after which STEM innovation rates will grind to a halt.

The Amish and Haredim double in number every twenty years; the Amish have done so for over a century. Christians took over the Roman Empire by doubling every twenty years for 300yrs, and these new insular religious subcultures seem similarly on track to replace our main world civilization. If you like what these subcultures stand for, and they let you join or influence them, then you can win. That is like folks on a ship heading for an iceberg, who get off onto lifeboats. The rest of us, in contrast, must grab the helm, to turn the ship of world culture, or go down with that ship.

Thankfully, human extinction seems unlikely. But the world might lose many key features of today’s world culture that were rare in prior cultures. Like democracy, pacifism, gender equality, anti-kid-beating, or open intellectual inquiry. If you want such features to last long into the future, well past your lifetime, you’ll need to mix them into adaptive cultures. As only adaptive cultures last.

We won’t be able to save much of our current culture, as much of it is likely maladaptive. Such as the proximate causes of fertility decline: long inflexible school paths, gender equality, capstone marriage, intensive parenting, distant grandparents, urbanization, and loss of religion. It is like if an invading army came to your city, and you had one hour to pack one suitcase, then leave. You’d think carefully about what to pack, but you couldn’t take much. Me, I most want to save open intellectual inquiry.

Our civilization may fall so far as to fragment, and restart strong selection via big wars, famines, and pandemics. Which could restart evolution, allowing a new world civilization to rise. But unless we find new ways to get key info re how to adapt, besides mass death and fragmentation, Earth civs may keep falling and rising indefinitely. Even getting human level AI won’t solve our culture evolution problem.

I see three promising approaches: (1) let capitalism [run](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/capitalist-voluntary) most all life areas, (2) run small groups [by](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/toward-adaption-futures) speculative market estimates of future group adaptive success, or (3) run big groups [by](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/futarchy-futurism) such price estimates of achieving big goals in conflict with civilization collapse, like when do 1M people live in space. The first two approaches face strong headwinds of widespread sentiment against both capitalism and Social Darwinism.

All three approaches require strong selection among market traders, who produce the info that can let groups stay adaptive without their frequent death or division. We will need to learn to direct cultural change, as we today direct many kinds of innovation. Maybe start [by](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/culture-guiding-futarchy) using markets to guide corporate cultures away from maladaption.
